https://whbl.com/2026/08/11/romania-dest.text: Sign In Search NEWS WEATHER EVENTS OBITUARIES CLOSINGS MORE AGRICULTURE BLOGS LOCAL SPORTS ON AIR PODCASTS Romania destroys drones drifting near major offshore gas project in the Black Sea By Thomson Reuters Aug 11, 2026 | 1:08 PM BUCHAREST, Aug 11 (Reuters) – Romanian army divers destroyed two Gerbera-type drones drifting in the country’s Black Sea exclusive economic zone near the offshore gas project Neptun Deep, ​Defence Minister Radu Miruta said on Tuesday. The NATO ‌state shares a 614-km (382-mile) land border with Ukraine and has seen Russian drones repeatedly breach its airspace over the last four years, as well as mines floating in the Black Sea across key trade and ‌energy ​routes. In July, Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots ⁠shot down three Russian ⁠drones breaching national airspace over three consecutive days after dozens of such incursions in the more than four years of Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine. On Tuesday, a civilian vessel working ​near the Neptun Deep offshore gas project spotted the drones, Miruta said. The minister did not specify the origin ⁠of the drones, but said Ukraine ⁠had confirmed they did not belong to its ​forces. “For the safety of the shipping lane and the works ​being carried out around the platform, the decision was ‌made to carry out a controlled destruction by detonation,” Miruta said. “The defence ministry contacted Ukrainian partners, who confirmed that the systems do not belong to them.” NATO states Romania, Bulgaria and Turkey, ⁠which share the Black Sea with Georgia, Russia and Ukraine, have neutralised more than 150 mines drifting across crucial trade lanes. In July, ⁠the three states ‌agreed to expand a joint task force ⁠that clears mines floating in the Black ​Sea to ‌include missions to protect critical infrastructure. All three ​countries have ⁠gas exploration or production projects in the Black Sea. Romania’s Neptun Deep, jointly owned by OMV Petrom and state gas producer Romgaz, is due to come onstream in 2027 and make Romania the European Union’s largest gas producer. https://www.politico.eu/article/france-g.text: PARIS — French presidential candidate Gabriel Attal said that if he wins the race to succeed Emmanuel Macron next year, he would move into the Elysée Palace with his romantic partner, EU industry chief Stéphane Séjourné. “We live together,” he said in an interview on French broadcaster LCI on Tuesday . “But again, we each have our paths, our trajectories. We have no intention of changing that.” Attal and Séjourné’s relationship poses a potential conflict of interest given the latter’s job as a European commissioner. Séjourné swore an oath upon taking office to prioritize EU interests over national matters, and his term runs beyond the French presidential election in April 2027. Advertisement Advertisement Attal, who leads Macron’s centrist party Renaissance, did not address — nor was he questioned in the interview — that potential conflict. Spokespersons for the two politicians both declined to comment for this story. But Attal said in his interview that he and Séjourné, who both rose to prominence while working for Macron, keep their careers separate. “We have always separated our careers. We are two public figures, but we don’t put ourselves on show together … we each follow our own paths separately,” he said. The pair were in a civil partnership from 2017 to 2022, while Attal held several ministerial positions — including government spokesperson — and Séjourné was an adviser to Macron before becoming an MEP. They then broke up for two years, before rekindling their relationship in 2024 . Recent polls show Attal trailing both front-runner and leader of the far-right National Rally Marine Le Pen and his main ideological rival, former Prime Minister and centrist contender Edouard Philippe, in the presidential race. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-ukrainian-d.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MuT6 Smoke was seen rising from a refinery near Moscow Image: REUTERS Advertisement Two people were killed in a Ukrainian drone attack on the Moscow region, local authorities said Sunday, with an oil refinery in the region also being hit. Energy infrastructure has been repeatedly targeted by both Ukraine and Russia , despite US President Donald Trump saying both sides had agreed to stop . Ukraine's repeated targeting of oil refineries has led to oil product shortages and fuel price increases in Russia. Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the strike had "a very significant impact," saying the oil in the hit refinery funds "billions of dollars to sustain the war machine." "Moscow must end its brutal war and choose peace instead of building layered rings of air defense at the expense of other regions," Zelenskyy posted on X. According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, more than 1,600 drones have been intercepted by Russia since Saturday, including 450 aimed at the Russian capital, making it one the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on the city since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. Moscow mayor accuses Ukraine of trying to disrupt parliamentary election Sobyanin said that numerous drones had made it to the oil refinery, and another one hit an apartment. The scale of the damage done to the refinery has not been confirmed. This comes as Russia is entering the last day of its three-day parliamentary election . Sobyanin said the "unprecedented attack was clearly planned with the aim of disrupting the elections." Meanwhile, in the eastern Ukrainian, Russian-occupied region of Kherson, a drone attack on a bus had killed two people, including an election official, Russian state news agency RIA reported. War anxiety casts shadow over Russia's election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Three children killed in Kyiv region In Ukraine, four people were killed in a Russian drone attack in the Kyiv region, local authorities said. Among the casualties are a mother and her two 3-year-old children, as well as a girl who was taken to hospital in another district and later died. The southwestern Fastiv district suffered damage to homes and industrial buildings. Russia's Defense Ministry said a warehouse of drone and missile maker Fire Point was struck in the Kyiv region. It also hit a cargo vessel and a postal logistics center in the Odesa region, saying both were used for military shipments. Russia has been repeatedly carrying out drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital in recent weeks. Earlier this month, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada’s formal application to join the force. ADRIAN DENNIS/Reuters Comments Share Save for later Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create Free Account Canada’s chief of the defence staff Jennie Carignan says joining a British-led rapid response force would help the Canadian Armed Forces put their new equipment and organizational structures to the test, while one expert cautions Ottawa may be stretching itself and its military too thin through a flurry of commitments. The Joint Expeditionary Force, currently made up of 10 NATO countries to respond quickly to emerging threats, would give Canada’s Armed Forces a “menu of options” in terms of opportunities to test new capabilities that the country is acquiring, General Carignan told The Globe and Mail. This includes drones and counter-drone technologies. “As we are onboarding new capabilities, there are opportunities to build exercise scenarios to integrate those new capabilities, and that is the advantage that participating in the JEF brings,” she said. The JEF was originally launched in 2014 by seven NATO members as a flexible, rapidly deployable force that could be used by participating countries to respond to crises as they see fit, saving them from having to put together a new unit every time. Its members currently include Britain, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. Given the geopolitics of its member countries, the force and its exercises have a heavy regional focus on Baltic and northern security. Canada and Britain in talks to merge defence financing initiatives, source says Prime Minister Mark Carney announced Canada’s formal application to join the force on Sept. 16, after a meeting with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Liverpool. Mr. Carney said Ottawa’s interest in joining the British-led force is part of an effort to reinforce Canada’s “military interoperability” and “collective security.” Canada’s submission to join the JEF comes after its previous involvement in the force’s activities, including Exercise TARASSIS in the fall of 2025. There, the Royal Canadian Air Force practised operating in contested, degraded and limited environments, for instance, by landing CF-18 fighter aircraft on a highway in Estonia. As well, Mr. Carney participated in a virtual meeting of the JEF in March to discuss the security of the Canadian Arctic, Northern Europe and the Baltic region. By nature, the JEF is meant to be a flexible organization that operates on an opt-in basis, said Robbie Boyd, a former senior military officer within Britain’s Ministry of Defence, who led the creation of the JEF in 2014. “It’s a strategic co-operation forum for defence development, for supporting each other, for discussion, and then it has that operational edge as well,” he told The Globe. For example, Mr. Boyd described the JEF’s first operation shortly after it was created to respond to an outbreak of the Ebola virus. Led by Britain, the country worked alongside its JEF partners Denmark and the Netherlands to deploy aid overseas. “Suddenly, we had this instant response of capabilities that we were able to build into the Ebola crisis.” The voluntary nature of the JEF appeals to Gen. Carignan, who said Canada would participate in exercises and missions based upon what it deems beneficial to its own Forces and their development. “The way this works is [JEF] planners get together, they figure out the schedule of events over the next cycle of exercises, and then nations make a decision on what force package they could have participate,” she said. Opinion: Canada must harden its defensive posture by joining the Joint Expeditionary Force Training with new drones that the Forces are acquiring, as well as participating in winter warfare exercises, are two specific goals Gen. Carignan highlighted for Canada if it joins the JEF. She added that Canada has lots to offer other JEF countries as well, such as training areas at Forces bases in Alberta and Newfoundland. But Canada’s contribution to any new force or strategic partnership will be limited by its own military capacity, said David Perry, president of the Canadian Global Affairs Institute, a think tank focused on international relations. Take the Royal Canadian Air Force, for example, which doesn’t have enough pilots to staff the 88 fighter jets that Ottawa is considering purchasing, he said. Or the navy, which is searching for submariners to staff its expanding submarine fleet . The federal government has signed a dozen or so memorandums of understanding and partnership agreements in the past year and a bit, Mr. Perry said. At some point, it’s going to have to be more selective and assess what’s actually going to stick. “Otherwise, I worry that we’re going to get distracted and spread way too thin,” he said. However, that doesn’t necessarily mean the federal government is wrong to think ahead. As military training and procurement chugs along, Mr. Perry said planning for the future is still the right call. “Otherwise, you wait too long and arrangements get solidified, and Canada will be on the outside looking in.” Report an editorial error Report a technical issue Editorial code of conduct Related stories Canada should hold on to military relationship with U.S., former defence chief says Trump has done ‘more than anyone’ to protect Canada, White House says Carney prepared for risk that Trump might order military action against Canada, report says Canada should hold on to military relationship with U.S., former defence chief says Trump has done ‘more than anyone’ to protect Canada, White House says Carney prepared for risk that Trump might order military action against Canada, report says Diversions Horoscope Daily astrology with Sally Brompton Daily Crossword Solve today's puzzle Daily Cryptic Witty word play at its best Sudoku Three difficulty levels to solve Follow related authors and topics Pippa Norman Follow You must be logged in to follow. Take steps now to protect tender plants from the cold. && Close Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save ASHLAND, Ore. - The Ashland New Plays Festival announced its complete lineup for the 34th annual Fall Festival, running Oct. 14-18 at Southern Oregon University's Main Stage Theatre. The festival showcases four new works brought to life by professional actors and directors. Playwrights workshop their scripts with professionals, often for the first time, and connect with audiences during talk-backs following each reading. According to the Ashland New Plays Festival, the winning scripts are selected through a community-based reading process. A group of theatre lovers volunteers their time to read each script without knowing the author's identity. Over six months, all 350 plays are read, debated and narrowed down based on content, originality and impact. Executive Artistic Director Jackie Apodaca selects the four winners. This year's festival features stories exploring memory, civil rights, family bonds and the threshold of life and death. "Netta and Ru" by Lisa Langford performs Wednesday, Oct. 14 at 7:30 p.m. and Saturday, Oct. 17 at 1:30 p.m. The play is set in Montgomery, Alabama in 1955 and follows Ruby, a hoodoo practitioner and sex worker who lost her magic after burying her mother. When her devout play-sister Netta gets engaged, their bond is tested as a murder brings a mysterious stranger to town and the historic bus boycott ignites around them. "Most people don't know the history of the Montgomery Bus Boycott beyond Rosa Parks and Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King," Langford said. "To overlook the women and queer people who were part of that struggle is to overlook the diversity that makes this country exceptional." Stori Ayers directs the production. The cast includes Adebowale Adebiyi, Ava Mingo, Trinity Ross and TayLar. "Persian Girl Play" by Ida Esmaeili performs Thursday, Oct. 15 at 1:30 p.m. and Friday, Oct. 16 at 7:30 p.m. The play follows a tight-knit group of Iranian teenagers in a small town outside of New York City who come together over a spring semester to fall in love, read fortunes in coffee and complain about their Persian parents. "I hope audiences feel like their worlds have gotten a bit bigger," Esmaeili said. "Mine definitely feels bigger because of this play." Melory Mirashrafi directs. The cast includes Awni Abdi-Bahri, Lily Gilan James, Isan Salem and Ava Yaghmaie. "Threshold" by Stephanie Fybel performs Thursday, Oct. 15 at 7:30 p.m. and Sunday, Oct. 18 at 1:30 p.m. as the festival's closing performance. The play follows respected appellate judge and Holocaust scholar David Lewin as he nears the end of his life, slipping in a morphine haze between the present and ghostly visits from his parents fleeing Nazi Germany and Lithuania in the late 1930s. "My father spent the last month of his life in a kind of a doorway; not yet gone but not fully here either," Fybel said. "I sat with him many nights wondering if the space between doorways, that threshold—between life and death, past and present, staying and leaving—is as narrow as we assume." Director Domenique Lozano said she's excited to examine the play's themes of justice, history, agency and courage. The cast includes Julia Gibbs, Anthony Heald, Brian Herndon, Shane Howard, Jane Ives, David Kelly and Barret O'Brien. "The Caelumids" by DJ Hills performs Friday, Oct. 16 at 1:30 p.m. and Saturday, Oct. 17 at 7:30 p.m. The play follows Blythe and Thora sitting on Blythe's porch talking about the future while their grandsons, Eddie and Mitchell, stand in the yard talking about the past. "I'm trans and I consider The Caelumids a work of trans theater even though all of the characters in the play, as far as they tell us, are cis," Hills said. "Part of what excites me about The Caelumids is how the play adheres to and breaks modes of realism—a genre that I steal from and resist in equal measure." Adam Sussman directs. The cast includes Vilma Silva and Robin Goodrin Nordli. The festival includes special events. An annual playwriting workshop led by host playwrights Beth Kander and E.M. Lewis takes place Saturday, Oct. 17 from 9 a.m. to noon at the Hay-Patton Rehearsal Center. A closing reception follows the final performance on Sunday, Oct. 18. O'Brien shared his perspective on what audiences can expect. "In the great tradition of new play festivals, ANPF tightens the aperture to focus squarely on the work: a bare stage, a few chairs, and the words -- the glorious, sparkly, new words," O'Brien said. "It's a thrill to be part of. A thrill that is felt across the stage and throughout the house." Tickets and information about special events can be found by clicking here .
